newsitem.title: UK: Britain and its leaders remember war dead.
newsitem.headline: Britain and its leaders remember war dead.

text.p: Britain remembered those who died in the two world wars in a moving ceremony led by Queen Elizabeth in the heart of London on Sunday and at other services across the country.
But royal matriarch, Queen Mother Elizabeth, now 96 and a symbol of Britain's wartime unity and defiance, was forced to stay at home.
Aides said she had a chill. "She hoped to be there and she is very disappointed," one aide said.

The queen was joined by Prime Minister John Major, Labour leader Tony Blair and other politicians and members of the royal family, as well as former premiers Margaret Thatcher, Edward Heath and James Callaghan for the London ceremony.
The queen placed a wreath on the Cenotaph memorial close to parliament before thousands of ex-servicemen and women, some in wheelchairs, marched past in tribute to their fallen comrades.
The balcony overlooking the ceremony which had been reserved for Queen Mother Elizabeth was left empty.

The ceremony, transmitted live on television, began with two minutes of silence. Shoppers in supermarkets, travellers at London's airports and people celebrating their own remembrance ceremonies across the country joined in the silence.
Another silence is expected to be observed by millions at home and in their workplaces on Monday.
Monday's silence -- at the start of the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month -- follows a campaign by veterans to revive the tradition to mark Armistice Day on November 11.

The campaign sought to build on the surge of emotion unleashed by last year's displays of remembrance to mark the 50th anniversary of the end of the war and to ensure today's youth do not forget the devastating conflicts.
